pharm: Orally active, non-peptide selective AT1-receptor antagonist that blocks the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-secreting effects of angiotensin II to lower blood pressure
tags: Boxed warning: fetal toxicity (discontinue when pregnancy detected)

summary: Irbesartan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) indicated for treatment of hypertension to lower blood pressure and reduce cardiovascular risk, and for treatment of diabetic nephropathy in hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes, elevated serum creatinine, and proteinuria. It is an orally active agent that does not require biotransformation and selectively antagonizes the AT1 receptor, blocking the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-secreting effects of angiotensin II. For hypertension the usual dose is 150 mg once daily, titrated to 300 mg as needed; for diabetic nephropathy the recommended dose is 300 mg once daily. Because it acts on the renin-angiotensin system, it carries a boxed warning for fetal toxicity and must be discontinued as soon as pregnancy is detected. Key risks include symptomatic hypotension in volume- or salt-depleted patients, worsening renal function in susceptible individuals, and hyperkalemia (notably in the diabetic nephropathy population); it is otherwise generally well tolerated and is not associated with the dry cough seen with ACE inhibitors.
indications: Treatment of hypertension in adults, to lower blood pressure (alone or with other antihypertensive agents)
Blood pressure lowering reduces the risk of fatal and nonfatal cardiovascular events, primarily strokes and myocardial infarctions
Treatment of diabetic nephropathy in hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes, an elevated serum creatinine, and proteinuria (>300 mg/day), to slow progression of nephropathy

moa: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor formed from angiotensin I by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, kininase II) and is the primary vasoactive hormone of the renin-angiotensin system, also stimulating aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex. Irbesartan blocks the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-secreting effects of angiotensin II by selectively binding to the AT1 angiotensin II receptor in tissues such as vascular smooth muscle and the adrenal gland. It is a specific competitive antagonist with more than 8500-fold greater affinity for the AT1 receptor than for the AT2 receptor and no agonist activity. Blockade of the AT1 receptor removes the negative feedback of angiotensin II on renin secretion, raising plasma renin activity and circulating angiotensin II, but this does not overcome the blood-pressure-lowering effect. Irbesartan does not inhibit ACE or renin and does not affect other receptors or ion channels involved in blood pressure and sodium homeostasis.

preg: Irbesartan can cause fetal harm and carries a boxed warning. Use of drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system during the second and third trimesters reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death; resulting oligohydramnios can be associated with fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformations, and potential neonatal effects include skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure, and death. When pregnancy is detected, discontinue irbesartan as soon as possible. If there is no appropriate alternative, apprise the mother of the potential risk to the fetus and perform serial ultrasounds to assess the intra-amniotic environment, though oligohydramnios may not appear until after irreversible fetal injury; if observed, consider alternative treatment. Closely observe exposed infants for hypotension, oliguria, and hyperkalemia; exchange transfusion or dialysis may be required. Hypertension in pregnancy itself raises maternal and fetal risk and should be managed accordingly. US general-population background risk of major birth defects is 2-4% and miscarriage 15-20%.
lact: There are no available data on the presence of irbesartan in human milk, effects on milk production, or effects on the breastfed infant. Irbesartan or a metabolite is secreted in the milk of lactating rats. Because of the potential for adverse effects on the nursing infant, use of irbesartan in breastfeeding women is not recommended.
renal: The pharmacokinetics of irbesartan are not altered in patients with renal impairment or in patients on hemodialysis, and irbesartan is not removed by hemodialysis. No dosage adjustment is necessary in mild to severe renal impairment unless the patient is also volume depleted, in which case a 75 mg starting dose is recommended. As a consequence of inhibiting the renin-angiotensin system, changes in renal function including acute renal failure may occur in patients whose renal function depends on RAAS activity (e.g., renal artery stenosis, chronic kidney disease, severe heart failure, volume depletion); monitor renal function periodically and consider withholding or discontinuing therapy if a clinically significant decline occurs. In the diabetic nephropathy population, irbesartan slows the doubling of serum creatinine and progression to end-stage renal disease.
hepatic: The pharmacokinetics of irbesartan after repeated oral administration are not significantly affected in patients with mild to moderate cirrhosis of the liver. No dosage adjustment is necessary in patients with hepatic insufficiency.

major: Aliskiren - do not coadminister in patients with diabetes; avoid in renal impairment (GFR <60 mL/min) due to hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal failure risk
Other RAS inhibitors (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) - dual RAS blockade increases risk of hypotension, hyperkalemia, and changes in renal function with little added benefit; generally avoid combined use
Lithium - increases serum lithium concentrations and risk of lithium toxicity; monitor lithium levels
moderate: NSAIDs including selective COX-2 inhibitors - may cause deterioration of renal function (including acute renal failure) in elderly, volume-depleted, or renally compromised patients, and may attenuate the antihypertensive effect; monitor renal function
Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, or potassium-containing salt substitutes and other agents that raise potassium - additive hyperkalemia; monitor serum potassium
minor: CYP2C9 substrates/inhibitors (sulfaphenazole, tolbutamide, nifedipine) inhibit oxidized irbesartan metabolite formation in vitro, but warfarin pharmacodynamics were negligibly affected clinically; no clinically significant interaction with hydrochlorothiazide, digoxin, or nifedipine
interactions.food: May be administered with or without food; food does not affect the bioavailability of irbesartan.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction described; limit alcohol as it may potentiate the blood-pressure-lowering effect and orthostatic hypotension.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum potassium (notably in diabetic nephropathy) and serum creatinine; postmarketing reports include increased liver function tests and increased CPK.

common: Dizziness (more frequent in diabetic nephropathy: 10.2% vs 6.0%)
Orthostatic dizziness and orthostatic hypotension (diabetic nephropathy population)

Hyperkalemia (potassium >6 mEq/L in 18.6% vs 6.0% placebo in IDNT; 2.1% discontinued)
Worsening renal function / acute renal failure in susceptible patients
rare: Hepatitis, jaundice, increased liver function tests

monitoring: Blood pressure response (effect apparent after first dose, near-full by 2 weeks)
Serum creatinine and renal function, particularly in patients with renal artery stenosis, CKD, heart failure, or volume depletion, and when used with NSAIDs or other RAS inhibitors
Serum potassium for hyperkalemia, especially in type 2 diabetic nephropathy patients
Volume and salt status before initiation
Serum lithium levels during concomitant lithium use
Signs of pregnancy in women of childbearing potential - discontinue if pregnancy detected
counsel: Take once daily, with or without food, at about the same time each day
Women of childbearing age should be advised of the consequences of exposure during pregnancy; report pregnancy to your physician as soon as possible and discuss options if planning pregnancy
Report lightheadedness, especially in the first days of therapy; if fainting occurs, stop the drug and contact your physician
Report inadequate fluid intake, excessive sweating, vomiting, or diarrhea, which can cause an excessive fall in blood pressure
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium without consulting your healthcare provider
Inform your physician of all other medicines, especially diuretics, NSAIDs, lithium, or other blood-pressure drugs
pk: Effect apparent after the first dose; complete (100%) inhibition of angiotensin II pressor response 4 hours after 150-300 mg, near-full antihypertensive effect by 2 weeks
Peak plasma concentrations attained at 1.5 to 2 hours after oral dosing; absolute bioavailability 60-80%
Terminal elimination half-life averages 11 to 15 hours
Once-daily dosing; steady state within 3 days, accumulation <20%; about 20% of radioactivity recovered in urine and remainder in feces
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions permitted 15-30 C (59-86 F)
pearls: Boxed warning for fetal toxicity - as a RAAS-acting drug, discontinue as soon as pregnancy is detected; second/third-trimester exposure can cause oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, and death
Dual indication: 150-300 mg once daily for hypertension and a fixed 300 mg once daily for type 2 diabetic nephropathy (slows doubling of serum creatinine and progression to ESRD per IDNT)
Use a 75 mg starting dose and correct volume/salt depletion in patients on high-dose diuretics or hemodialysis to avoid symptomatic hypotension
Hyperkalemia is notably more common in the diabetic nephropathy population (K >6 mEq/L in ~19% in IDNT) - monitor potassium closely
Orally active and does not require biotransformation; metabolized via glucuronidation and CYP2C9 oxidation, not removed by hemodialysis, and not associated with ACE-inhibitor dry cough
Avoid dual RAS blockade (with ACE inhibitors, other ARBs, or aliskiren) - increased hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal failure with little added benefit
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered on the same day. If it is almost time for the next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: No human overdose data are available, although daily doses of 900 mg for 8 weeks were well tolerated. The most likely manifestations of overdose are hypotension and tachycardia; bradycardia may also occur. Management is supportive and directed by the patient's clinical status. Irbesartan is not removed by hemodialysis.
